claims.text: Annealing equimolar CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles at 300–350 °C preferentially segregates Mn to their surfaces.
Mn is a lower-melting-point constituent whose segregation governs surface premelting in CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles.
Equimolar CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles can be produced by ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation in liquid.
The as-synthesized CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles have a uniform, homogeneous elemental distribution.
A temperature of 300–350 °C is below the bulk melting point of the alloy.
Annealing at 300–350 °C for up to 60 minutes can selectively alter the surface composition without changing the nanoparticle core.
Differences in surface free energy and cohesive energy drive constituent segregation to HEA nanoparticle surfaces.
For CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles, differential surface free energies specifically drive Mn migration to the surface.
Mn enrichment at the surface lowers the local cohesive energy.
Low-cohesion, chemically soft surface regions initiate melting earlier than homogeneous surface regions.
Melting initiated at segregated surface regions propagates inward as temperature increases.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will have a statistically significantly lower premelting-onset temperature than homogeneous controls.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will develop a thicker premelting layer than homogeneous controls.
The proposed segregation-controlled premelting effect holds for CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles approximately 5–30 nm in diameter.
At conditions beyond 300–350 °C or 60 minutes, core diffusion or sintering may complicate the thermal behavior.
